children: By Karishma Vanjani
Bonds peddled by the U.S. government are declining in value again, and the offender has a familiar face: expected Federal Reserve rate hikes.
The 10-year Treasury was yielding above 5% on Tuesday, though it settled a hair below that. When prices fall, yields rise.

Bond prices sagged for much of this year, and yields on the 10-year Treasury soared to 5.31% in early October. Then bonds staged a sharp rebound — October ended up being the best month for Treasuries since December 2023. Positive momentum continued on in November as investors moved away from risky stocks to bonds, keeping yields below 5% over the past seven days. Alas, it was all short-lived.
The culprit for the selloff?
"The simplest, and correct answer is Fed rate hikes," said Barry Knapp, founder of Ironsides Macroeconomics.
Odds of a Fed hike in December now look near certain compared with 68% early last week, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.

Early Tuesday morning, Fed Governor Christopher Waller had suggested a half-percentage point increase in interest rates is possible in December. Later, inflation data came out strong and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan backed him up, saying at least two additional quarter-point increases are needed to rein in prices. Two other Fed officials, Beth Hammack and Tom Barkin, also made a case for hikes last week.
Strong jobs data on Friday also suggested the Fed has room to hike rates without damaging the labor market.

These same forces have pushed up Treasury yields most of this year. "Our analysis shows the increase in 10s in '26 was primarily driven by the Fed policy path," Barry said. Research by Morgan Stanley, published Friday, also showed that expectations of where Fed takes interest rates "remains the most important input to a 10-year yield forecast."
There is a silver lining to Tuesday's bond selloff.

Higher interest rates can bring down inflation over the long-term — and investors are increasingly confident the Fed will pull it off. Look at the 10-year break-evens, the bond market's gauge of average expected annual inflation over the next decade. It has fallen steeply since late September to now sit at its lowest level since July 28 at 2.217% on Tuesday.
"Break-evens are stable because the Fed has credibility and is viewed as independent," said Priya Misra, Core Plus Bond ETF portfolio manager at J.P. Morgan.

Further confirmation lies in another U.S. government bond, the 10-year Treasury inflation-protected security. The yield on TIPS strips out inflation. Because the 10-year TIPS yield and the yield on a traditional 10-year Treasury rose by almost the same amount on Tuesday, it means inflation expectations didn't change.
The big question now is whether long-dated yields push higher from here — even though inflation forecasts are declining.

"The answer is yes, they could," said Padhraic Garvey, regional head of Americas research at ING. A strong economy evidenced by gross domestic product growth and a growing federal budget deficit are among the factors that could get yields on the route to 6%, he said.

Garvey said he would be tempted to "cap the upside at 5.5%." In simple English that means: Buy bonds when yields reach an expected peak of 5.5%. Fair value is between 4.5% to 5.25%, according to Priya, who sees a potential for Treasury rallying if artificial intelligence stocks get hammered again, especially with Anthropic's market debut around the corner.

For investors that are willing to hold bonds until they mature, this is as good a time as any to get in and secure the high yields. In recent days, the market has gotten closer to the October peak of 5.31% in 10-year yields.

But traders — who huff and puff over every basis point move in yields — need psychological fortitude. There are enough reasons to keep yields elevated in the near-term that traders betting on a decline could get burned.
"The pressure on government bonds might continue in the near term, [but] we doubt it will last long," wrote Capital Economics' Chief Economic Advisor John Higgins on Tuesday.
Wall Street's year-end forecast for the 10-year are clustered around 4.8%-5%, and it's a fools errand to forecast longer than that.
